name: Italy
title: Italy: income-based fees and regional grants that make study nearly free
lede: Italian public universities set tuition by family income, and regional student-aid agencies give grants, fee exemptions and housing to students with limited means — including international students. Merit scholarships add another route.
description: How international students can study in Italy for little or nothing: income-based fees, regional DSU grants such as ER.GO in Bologna, and merit awards at Politecnico di Milano.
card: Fees scale with family income, and regional DSU grants can waive them and add up to about €7,000 a year.

sections.html: Italian public universities calculate most students' fees from family income and assets, using an indicator called the ISEE (for families abroad, an equivalent calculated from home-country documents). Students from lower-income families pay little or nothing, and some universities offer reduced flat fees to students from developing countries.

Each Italian region funds a student-aid agency that awards the diritto allo studio (DSU) scholarship. In Emilia-Romagna, where the University of Bologna is, the agency is ER.GO. For 2026–27 it offered a full fee exemption plus a grant of up to €7,171.11 a year for students living away from home, with access to student housing, for families with an ISEE of up to €25,000 and an ISPE of up to €50,000. Applications ran from late June to 24 August 2026.

Some universities reward strong international applicants directly. Politecnico di Milano waives tuition for top applicants to its English-taught master's programmes, and adds up to €10,000 a year for the highest-ranked — but only for applicants who apply in its Early Bird window (1 October to 1 December).

Income-based aid needs official documents about your family's income and property from your home country, usually translated and legalised. Start collecting them in spring: DSU windows close in late summer, often before international students arrive.

sections.h: Proof of funds for your visa
sections.html: For a study visa you must show at least €10,179.85 for the 2026–27 academic year, plus the cost of a return journey. The threshold is linked to Italy's social allowance and is updated each year. Consulates can ask for more, judging the whole financial situation of your family or sponsor, and some accept only certain kinds of evidence, so read the checklist of the consulate that handles your application.

With a study residence permit you can work up to 20 hours a week and 1,040 hours a year. After a bachelor's (laurea), master's (laurea magistrale), specialising master's or PhD, you can convert your study permit into a one-year residence permit while awaiting employment. Register with the local job centre (Centro per l'Impiego) first. During that year the permit can be changed into a work permit once you find a job.

faq.q: How much money do I need for an Italian student visa?
faq.a: At least €10,179.85 for 2026–27, plus money for a return journey. Consulates may ask for more evidence about your family's or sponsor's finances.

faq.q: Can I work while studying in Italy?
faq.a: Yes, up to 20 hours a week and 1,040 hours a year with a study residence permit.

faq.q: Can I stay in Italy after graduating?
faq.a: Yes. After a degree or PhD you can convert your permit into a one-year permit to look for work, after registering with the local job centre.
